A metric space is a space whre distance between points can be measured.

== Formal definition ==

Let $S$ be a set.

Function

$$
d: S \times S \to \mathbb{R}
$$

is a '''metric function''' of $S$ if

$$
\begin{cases}
d(a,b) \ge 0,\, \forall a,b \in S \text{  (Positive definiteness)} \\
d(a,b) = 0 \iff a=b \text{  (Non-overlay)} \\
d(a,b)=d(b,a),\,  \forall a,b \in S \text{  (Symmetry)} \\
d(a,c) \le d(a,b)+d(b,c),\, \forall a,b,c \in S \text{  (Triangle inequality)} \\
\end{cases};
$$

In which case $d(a,b)$ is called the '''distance''' between $a,b$; $(S,d)$ is a '''metric space''', often denoted by $\mathcal{X}$.

{{Hidden example}}
The '''discrete metric function''' for any set $S$ is:

$$
\forall a,b \in S,\, 
d(a,b)=
\begin{cases}
0,\, a=b \\
1,\, \text{elsewise}
\end{cases}
$$
{{End hidden}}

<ref>{{#cite:Q2293}}</ref>

== Isometry ==

Function

$$
f: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}
$$

is said to be '''distance-preserving''' if

$$
d_{\mathcal{Y}} (f(A), f(B)) = d_{\mathcal{X}} (A, B)
$$

and if it is also bijective,i.e.,

$$
\exists f^-1: \mathcal{Y} \to \mathcal{X},\, \forall y \in \mathcal{Y}, f^{-1}(y)=x \iff f(x)=y
$$

then $f$ is an '''isometry''' of metric space $\mathcal{X}$ to metric space $\mathcal{Y}$, and metric spaces $\mathcal{X,Y}$ are said to be '''isometric''' over $f$.

<ref>{{#cite:Q2296}}</ref>
